docs.title: About
docs.text:
Econometrics Simplified is a blog about the ideas behind applied econometrics, explained in plain words.

Each post takes one idea, wraps it in a small story, and runs the numbers in EViews. The data are simulated on purpose: because we know the truth that generated them, we can see exactly when a regression gets it right and when it is fooled.

Every post ends with a question. Leave your answer in the comments, argue with me, or tell me I'm wrong.

docs.title: About the author
docs.text:
Dr. Santhosh Kumar P.K. is Professor of Economics and Director at the Centre for Budget Studies, Cochin University of Science and Technology (CUSAT), Kochi, Kerala, India. Holding a Ph.D. in Economics, his academic and research focus spans quantitative econometrics, time-series modeling, and applied economic policy.

In addition to his extensive academic publications and regular policy columns in major national publications, Dr. Santhosh Kumar is deeply passionate about expanding accessible quantitative education. He offers popular online SWAYAM (IIM Bangalore) courses, including "Introduction to Financial Econometrics" and "Econometrics with R from Beginners to Analysts," helping learners bridge theoretical economics with practical computational tools.

docs.title: Does Ice Cream Drown People?
docs.text:
Here is a headline I would love to see in a newspaper: "Ice cream linked to drownings — every extra thousand litres sold costs lives." It sounds absurd. Yet the regression behind it would look perfectly respectable.

About this post

Concept: omitted variable bias · Data sheet: P1_icecream · Simulated monthly data, 2015M01–2024M12, 120 observations

Download the data (Excel) — sheet P1_icecream · EViews program

Let me show you.

docs.text:

  • DROWN — the number of drowning incidents
  • ICECREAM — ice cream sales, in thousand litres
  • TEMP — the average maximum temperature, in °C

A keen young analyst only has the first two series. She opens EViews and types ls drown c icecream.

docs.title: What went wrong?
docs.text:
Nothing in the arithmetic. Everything in the thinking.

On hot days, people buy ice cream. On hot days, people also go swimming. Temperature drives both series. Ice cream is simply standing in for the weather, like a witness who happened to be at the scene of the crime.

Econometricians call this omitted variable bias. When a variable that matters (temperature) is left out, and it is correlated with a variable we include (ice cream), the included variable quietly absorbs its effect.

The idea fits in one line. If the true model is

\[ DROWN = \beta_0 + \beta_1 ICECREAM + \beta_2 TEMP + u \]

and we leave out TEMP, then the slope we estimate on ICECREAM is not β1. It is β1 plus (β2 × how strongly TEMP moves with ICECREAM). Two things must both be true for the bias to appear: the omitted variable must affect the outcome, and it must be correlated with the included regressor.

docs.title: Confession
docs.text: I generated these data. In the true model, ice cream has zero effect on drownings. Temperature alone does the work. That is the beauty of simulation: we know the truth, so we can catch the regression lying.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text: A significant t-statistic tells you that a coefficient is precisely estimated. It does not tell you that the coefficient means what you want it to mean. Before you trust a slope, ask: what else moves with my X, and also moves my Y?

docs.title: Something to think about
docs.text: Studies often find that people who drink a little coffee live longer than people who drink none. List three omitted variables that could create this pattern. For each, say which way it would bias the coffee coefficient. Leave your answers in the comments.

docs.title: The Test That Needed Its Own Table: Dickey and Fuller
docs.text:
You want to know whether \(\rho = 1\). You know how to test whether a coefficient equals some number: run the regression, compute a t-statistic, look it up in the t-table at the back of the textbook. Simple.

Except that here, the t-table at the back of the textbook is wrong. Not slightly wrong. Wrong enough that if you trust it, you will "discover" stationarity in almost half of all random walks. This chapter is about the two statisticians from Iowa who worked out what the right table looks like.

Unit Root Series · Chapter 2 of 8

1. The kite and the balloon · 2. Dickey-Fuller · 3. Augmented Dickey-Fuller · 4. Phillips-Perron · 5. KPSS · 6. DF-GLS and Ng-Perron · 7. Structural breaks · 8. Panel unit roots

Data: blog_datasets.xlsx, sheet P10_dickey_fuller · Simulated monthly data, 2005M01–2024M12

docs.title: A small trick with a big name
docs.text:
Start from the AR(1) model of Chapter 1:

\[ y_t = \rho\, y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t \]

Subtract \(y_{t-1}\) from both sides:

\[ \underbrace{y_t - y_{t-1}}_{\Delta y_t} = (\rho - 1)\, y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t \]

Call \(\delta = \rho - 1\). Now the question "is \(\rho = 1\)?" becomes "is \(\delta = 0\)?":

\[ \Delta y_t = \delta\, y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t \qquad H_0: \delta = 0 \ (\text{unit root}) \quad \text{vs} \quad H_1: \delta < 0 \ (\text{stationary}) \]

Two things to notice:

  1. The test is one-sided. We only care about \(\delta < 0\). An explosive series with \(\rho > 1\), a balloon with a rocket attached, is not what economists usually worry about.
  2. The null hypothesis is the unit root. The test assumes "balloon" until the data prove otherwise. Keep this in mind; in Chapter 5 we will meet a test that does the exact opposite.

Run the regression, compute \(t = \hat\delta / \operatorname{se}(\hat\delta)\), and compare it with a critical value. The whole drama is about which critical value.

docs.title: Why the t-table lies
docs.text:
The ordinary t-test assumes the regressor behaves itself: it has a stable mean and variance. Under the null hypothesis, our regressor \(y_{t-1}\) is a random walk. Its variance grows with time, as we saw in Chapter 1. The usual theory breaks.

I simulated 20,000 random walks of length 100. For each one I ran the Dickey-Fuller regression with a constant and recorded the t-statistic. In every one of them the true \(\delta\) is exactly zero. Here is the distribution of those t-statistics, against the normal curve the textbook assumes:

The real distribution is shifted to the left and skewed. Its average is about −1.5, not 0. Its 5% point is −2.93, not −1.645.

Now the scary number: 45% of these t-statistics are below −1.645. If you used the ordinary one-sided t-table at 5%, you would declare a random walk "stationary" in 45 cases out of 100. Your "5% test" would actually be a 45% test.

Derivation: where the strange distribution comes from (click to open)

Take the simplest case, no constant, \(y_0 = 0\), and true \(\rho = 1\). The OLS estimate is

\[ \hat\rho - 1 = \frac{\sum y_{t-1}\varepsilon_t}{\sum y_{t-1}^2} \]

Look at the numerator. Because \(y_t = y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t\), squaring gives \(y_t^2 = y_{t-1}^2 + 2y_{t-1}\varepsilon_t + \varepsilon_t^2\), so

\[ y_{t-1}\varepsilon_t = \tfrac12\left(y_t^2 - y_{t-1}^2 - \varepsilon_t^2\right) \]

Add this up from \(t = 1\) to \(T\). The middle terms cancel like a telescope:

\[ \sum_{t=1}^{T} y_{t-1}\varepsilon_t = \tfrac12\left(y_T^2 - \sum_{t=1}^T \varepsilon_t^2\right) \]

Divide by \(T\sigma^2\). Since \(y_T\) is a sum of \(T\) shocks, \(y_T/(\sigma\sqrt{T})\) is approximately standard normal, so \(y_T^2/(T\sigma^2)\) is approximately \(\chi^2_1\). And \(\sum\varepsilon_t^2/(T\sigma^2) \to 1\). Therefore

\[ \frac{1}{T\sigma^2}\sum y_{t-1}\varepsilon_t \;\longrightarrow\; \tfrac12\left(\chi^2_1 - 1\right) \]

A \(\chi^2_1\) variable has mean 1 but median only 0.45. So \(\chi^2_1 - 1\) is negative more than two-thirds of the time. That is the source of the leftward shift: the numerator of \(\hat\rho - 1\) is usually negative even when the truth is \(\rho = 1\).

The denominator also does not settle down to a constant. In the language of advanced theory, both pieces converge to functionals of a Brownian motion \(W(r)\):

\[ T(\hat\rho - 1) \Rightarrow \frac{\tfrac12\left(W(1)^2 - 1\right)}{\int_0^1 W(r)^2\,dr} \]

Two more surprises hide in this formula. First, we multiply by \(T\), not \(\sqrt{T}\): the estimate of \(\rho\) converges to 1 faster than usual. Econometricians call this superconsistency. Second, the limit is a ratio of random quantities, not a normal distribution. No t-table can describe it, so someone had to simulate it.

docs.title: The two men from Iowa
docs.text:
That someone was David Dickey, a PhD student at Iowa State University, and his supervisor, Wayne Fuller.

Fuller is an unusual hero for a time-series story. He trained in agricultural economics at Iowa State, and he is best known as one of the giants of survey sampling: how to design and analyse surveys of farms, households and people. A conversation with him was published in the journal Survey Methodology in 2026, recounting his early life and his work, including the Dickey-Fuller test.

In the 1970s there were no laptops. There was also no formula that would give the critical values directly. So Dickey and Fuller did what I did for the chart above, on the slow computers of the day: they generated a large number of artificial random walks, ran the regression on each, and tabulated the results. The critical values appeared in Fuller's 1976 book Introduction to Statistical Time Series, and the theory in two papers: Dickey and Fuller (1979) in the Journal of the American Statistical Association, and (1981) in Econometrica. They are among the most cited papers in statistics.

David Dickey went on to a long career at North Carolina State University, where he is a William Neal Reynolds Professor of Statistics. Later, James MacKinnon of Queen's University in Canada used much larger simulations to fit formulas for the critical values at any sample size. That is why every EViews unit root output ends with the line "*MacKinnon (1996) one-sided p-values".

docs.title: Three versions of the test
docs.text:
Real series rarely wander around zero. So the regression comes in three flavours:

Version Regression Use when the series… 5% critical value (large samples) None \(\Delta y_t = \delta y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t\) wanders around zero −1.94 Constant \(\Delta y_t = \alpha + \delta y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t\) wanders around a non-zero level −2.86 Constant + trend \(\Delta y_t = \alpha + \beta t + \delta y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t\) has a clear upward or downward trend −3.41

Every deterministic term you add pushes the critical value further left. The test has to work harder to prove stationarity, because a constant and a trend can themselves mimic some of the wandering.

What does each version compare?
  • Constant: a random walk (with no drift) versus a stationary series around a fixed mean.
  • Constant + trend: a random walk with drift versus a stationary series around a straight-line trend. A random walk with drift, \(y_t = \mu + y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t\), can be written \(y_t = y_0 + \mu t + \sum \varepsilon_s\): a trend plus a balloon. A trend-stationary series is \(y_t = a + bt + u_t\) with \(u_t\) a kite. Both trend upwards. Only one of them ever returns to its trend line.

Never use the Prob. column of the test equation for the unit root coefficient. That number comes from the ordinary t-distribution, which is the very thing Dickey and Fuller showed does not apply. The only p-value that counts is the one at the top, 0.2205.

And the constant? In a stationary series, \(\alpha = (1-\rho)\mu\), so the long-run mean is \(\hat\mu = \hat\alpha / (1-\hat\rho) = 1.591 / 0.271 \approx 5.9\%\). The kite's home is just under 6%.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text:
The Dickey-Fuller regression looks like any other regression, but it lives in a different world. The coefficient on \(y_{t-1}\) must be judged against Dickey-Fuller critical values, not against the t-table. A test statistic of −2.5 that would make you famous in an ordinary regression means nothing here.

There is a catch that we have ignored so far: we assumed the gusts of wind \(\varepsilon_t\) are independent from one minute to the next. In real data they rarely are. Fixing that is the job of Chapter 3.

Something to think about

The test always starts from "unit root" and needs strong evidence to reject it. With only 30 years of annual data, what do you expect to happen when the true \(\rho\) is 0.9? Is "I could not reject a unit root" the same as "I found a unit root"? Answer in the comments; Chapter 6 has the numbers.

docs.title: Giving the Test a Memory: The Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test
docs.text:
The plain Dickey-Fuller test makes one heroic assumption: the shocks that push the series around are completely unpredictable, like coin tosses. Real economies are not like that. A good quarter for business tends to be followed by another good quarter. Monsoon effects spill over several months. If yesterday's shock tells you something about today's, the Dickey-Fuller test is reading the wrong table again.

The cure, invented by Said E. Said and David Dickey, is almost embarrassingly simple: give the regression a memory.

Unit Root Series · Chapter 3 of 8

1. The kite and the balloon · 2. Dickey-Fuller · 3. Augmented Dickey-Fuller · 4. Phillips-Perron · 5. KPSS · 6. DF-GLS and Ng-Perron · 7. Structural breaks · 8. Panel unit roots

Data: blog_datasets.xlsx, sheet P11_adf · Simulated quarterly data, 1995Q1–2024Q4

docs.title: Where the extra terms come from
docs.text:
Suppose the series depends on its last two values, an AR(2):

\[ y_t = \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t \]

Let's rewrite it with the same trick as in Chapter 2. Add and subtract \(\phi_2 y_{t-1}\) on the right-hand side:

\[ y_t = (\phi_1 + \phi_2)\, y_{t-1} - \phi_2 (y_{t-1} - y_{t-2}) + \varepsilon_t \]

Now subtract \(y_{t-1}\) from both sides:

\[ \Delta y_t = \underbrace{(\phi_1 + \phi_2 - 1)}_{\delta}\, y_{t-1} \;\underbrace{-\,\phi_2}_{\gamma_1}\, \Delta y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t \]

This is the Dickey-Fuller regression with one extra term, the lagged change \(\Delta y_{t-1}\). And the unit root question is still the question "is \(\delta = 0\)?", because an AR(2) has a unit root exactly when \(\phi_1 + \phi_2 = 1\).

Why does \(\phi_1 + \phi_2 = 1\) mean a unit root?

The lag polynomial of an AR(2) is \(1 - \phi_1 z - \phi_2 z^2\). Put \(z = 1\): you get \(1 - \phi_1 - \phi_2\). If this is zero, then \(z = 1\) is a root of the polynomial. A unit root, by definition.

The same algebra works for any number of lags. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) regression is

\[ \Delta y_t = \alpha + \beta t + \delta\, y_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \gamma_j\, \Delta y_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t \]

The lagged changes soak up the short-run memory. What is left in \(\varepsilon_t\) is, we hope, pure noise again, and the t-statistic on \(\delta\) follows the same Dickey-Fuller distribution as before. That is the beauty of it: no new tables needed.

docs.title: A man named Said
docs.text:
In 1984 the journal Biometrika published "Testing for unit roots in autoregressive-moving average models of unknown order" by Said E. Said and David A. Dickey. They showed that even if the true process is more complicated than any finite AR, with moving-average parts as well, the ADF regression still works as long as the number of lags grows slowly with the sample size.

So the ADF test is, in a sense, what Said said. (Every econometrics teacher has made this joke. I could not resist either.)

docs.title: How many lags? The Goldilocks problem
docs.text:
Choosing \(p\) is the one real decision in an ADF test.

  • Too few lags: leftover autocorrelation in the residuals. The test statistic no longer follows the Dickey-Fuller distribution, and the test rejects too often or too rarely.
  • Too many lags: each extra lag costs a degree of freedom and blurs the estimate of \(\delta\). The test loses power, its ability to spot a kite.

The usual approach is to let an information criterion choose. EViews starts from a maximum lag given by Schwert's rule

\[ p_{\max} = \left\lfloor 12 \left(\frac{T}{100}\right)^{1/4} \right\rfloor \]

and picks the lag between 0 and \(p_{\max}\) with the smallest Schwarz Information Criterion (SIC). For 120 quarterly observations, \(p_{\max} = \lfloor 12 \times 1.2^{0.25}\rfloor = 12\). Ng and Perron (2001) proposed a "modified" criterion (MAIC) that behaves better when the series is close to a unit root; EViews offers it as an option.

docs.title: Which deterministic terms?
docs.text:
The second decision is whether to include a constant, or a constant and a trend. The rule of thumb is: look at the picture first. The test should be able to describe the series under both hypotheses.

A more formal route, the sequential procedure of Dolado, Jenkinson and Sosvilla-Rivero (1990), starts with the most general model and tests whether the trend can be dropped. In practice, the picture usually settles it.

docs.title: The data
docs.text: The sheet P11_adf has 30 years of quarterly data on LGDP, the natural log of real GDP for an imaginary economy. I built it as a random walk with drift: quarterly growth averages 1.5%, and growth itself is autocorrelated (a good quarter tends to be followed by another one, with \(\rho = 0.45\)). In truth, LGDP is I(1) and its growth rate is I(0).

docs.title: A note on "the trend is significant"
docs.text: Students often see that @TREND has a t-statistic of 1.85 and conclude something about the trend. Careful: in the ADF equation, the constant and trend coefficients also have non-standard distributions under the null. Dickey and Fuller (1981) tabulated separate critical values for them. As a rule, use the test equation to check the residuals and the lag terms, and use only the top half of the output for the unit root decision.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text:
The ADF test is the Dickey-Fuller test with a memory. Add enough lagged changes to clean up the residuals, but not so many that you blind the test. Then always ask the follow-up question: if the level has a unit root, is the first difference stationary?

Something to think about

Take a monthly series with a strong seasonal pattern, such as umbrella sales from Post 6. What would SIC need to do with the lags to capture a 12-month pattern? What could go wrong if the maximum lag were only 4? Tell me in the comments.

docs.title: The Two Phillipses: A Crocodile Hunter, a Water Computer, and the Phillips-Perron Test
docs.text:
New Zealand is a small country with a population of around five million. It has produced two of the most famous econometricians in history, and both of them are called Phillips. Neither is related to the other. One built a working model of the British economy out of water tanks and pipes. The other gave us the mathematics of wandering time series, including the unit root test in this chapter.

Let me introduce them, and then show you what the Phillips-Perron test does differently from the ADF.

Unit Root Series · Chapter 4 of 8

1. The kite and the balloon · 2. Dickey-Fuller · 3. Augmented Dickey-Fuller · 4. Phillips-Perron · 5. KPSS · 6. DF-GLS and Ng-Perron · 7. Structural breaks · 8. Panel unit roots

Data: blog_datasets.xlsx, sheet P12_phillips_perron · Simulated monthly data, 2005M01–2024M12

docs.title: Phillips number one: Bill
docs.text:
Alban William Housego Phillips, known as Bill, was born in 1914 at Te Rehunga, near Dannevirke, in New Zealand. He left school early and worked his way around Australia. Among his jobs: crocodile hunter and cinema manager.

In the Second World War he served with the Royal Air Force and was captured when Java fell to the Japanese. He spent about three and a half years in a prisoner-of-war camp. There he learned Chinese from other prisoners, and he repaired and miniaturised a secret radio so the prisoners could hear the news. He also built a little water boiler for tea that ran off the camp's lighting system.

After the war he studied at the London School of Economics. In 1949, over one summer, in his landlady's garage in Croydon, he built the MONIAC: a machine about two metres tall in which coloured water flows through tanks and pipes to show how income, spending, taxes and savings move around an economy. It cost about £400 to build. Somewhere between twelve and fourteen were made; one still works at the University of Cambridge, and others are on display at the Science Museum in London and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Museum.

In 1958 he published the paper that made his name immortal, on the relationship between unemployment and the rate of change of money wages in the UK. You know it as the Phillips curve. He died in Auckland in 1975.

docs.title: Phillips number two: Peter
docs.text:
Peter C. B. Phillips studied economics and mathematics at the University of Auckland and completed a PhD in econometrics at the LSE in 1974, the same school where Bill had built his water computer. He moved to Yale in 1979 and has been there ever since; he is now Sterling Professor Emeritus. He founded the journal Econometric Theory, has supervised more than 100 PhD students, and his papers have been cited well over 100,000 times. Much of what we know today about regressions with random walks comes from him.

In 1988 Peter Phillips and Pierre Perron published "Testing for a unit root in time series regression" in Biometrika. Perron will come back in Chapter 7 with one of the most famous papers in macroeconomics.

So: one Phillips poured water through pipes to show how the economy flows. The other Phillips wrote the theory of how economic series wander. Both studied at the LSE. Both came from New Zealand. If you ever need a pub quiz question for econometricians, you are welcome.

docs.title: The problem, again
docs.text:
Back in Chapter 3, the ADF test dealt with autocorrelated shocks by adding lagged differences to the regression. That is a parametric fix: we model the memory explicitly.

Phillips and Perron had a different idea. Keep the simple Dickey-Fuller regression with no lags at all:

\[ \Delta y_t = \alpha + \delta\, y_{t-1} + u_t \]

Let \(u_t\) be autocorrelated, or have changing variance, or both. Then correct the t-statistic afterwards for the damage this does. That is a non-parametric fix: we don't model the memory, we just measure how much of it there is.

docs.title: Short-run variance and long-run variance
docs.text:
The key idea is the difference between two variances of the residuals.

  • The short-run variance \(\gamma_0\): how big the shocks are in a single month.
  • The long-run variance \(f_0\): how big their accumulated effect is over many months.

If shocks are independent, these two are the same. If a positive shock tends to be followed by more positive shocks, the shocks pile up, and the long-run variance is bigger than the short-run variance. Think of rain: one heavy shower (short-run) is different from a week of showers that keep coming (long-run).

The long-run variance is estimated with a weighted sum of autocovariances, the Newey-West estimator with a Bartlett kernel:

\[ \hat f_0 = \hat\gamma_0 + 2\sum_{j=1}^{\ell} \left(1 - \frac{j}{\ell + 1}\right)\hat\gamma_j \]

where \(\hat\gamma_j\) is the autocovariance of the residuals at lag \(j\) and \(\ell\) is the bandwidth: how many lags we look at. EViews chooses \(\ell\) automatically.

The Phillips-Perron statistic, as EViews computes it, is

\[ \tilde t_\delta = t_\delta \left(\frac{\hat\gamma_0}{\hat f_0}\right)^{1/2} - \frac{T(\hat f_0 - \hat\gamma_0)\,\operatorname{se}(\hat\delta)}{2 \hat f_0^{1/2}\, s} \]

where \(t_\delta\) and \(\operatorname{se}(\hat\delta)\) are the t-statistic and standard error from the simple regression, and \(s\) is its standard error of regression. Don't panic at the formula. Look at what it does: if \(\hat f_0 = \hat\gamma_0\), the correction vanishes and you get back the ordinary Dickey-Fuller t-statistic. The bigger the gap between long-run and short-run variance, the bigger the correction. The corrected statistic uses the same Dickey-Fuller critical values.

  • arrive in bursts: a few calm years, then a few months of large shocks, like a market under stress.

So the truth is: SPREAD is a kite, but with untidy, autocorrelated, heteroskedastic gusts.

Let me walk through it.

The test equation at the bottom is the plain Dickey-Fuller regression. Its t-statistic on SPREAD(-1) is −2.75. On its own, against a 5% critical value of −2.87, that would not reject the unit root. But the Durbin-Watson stat of 1.12 warns that the residuals are autocorrelated, so the plain DF test is not reliable here.

The variances in the middle box tell the story. The residual variance is 0.053, but the HAC (long-run) variance is 0.077, about 44% larger. The shocks pile up.

The adjusted t-statistic is −3.32, with p = 0.014. After the correction, we reject the unit root at the 5% level. SPREAD is stationary, which is the truth.

For comparison, the ADF test with SIC lags (1 lag chosen) gives −4.68, p = 0.0001. Both fixes, the parametric and the non-parametric, reach the right answer here. The naive test, without any fix, would have got it wrong.

docs.title: ADF or PP?
docs.text:
ADF Phillips-Perron How it handles memory Adds lagged differences Corrects the t-statistic afterwards Choice you must make Number of lags Bandwidth (EViews automates it) Changing variance (heteroskedasticity) Not designed for it Robust to it Weak spot Wrong lag length Large negative moving-average shocks (the test rejects far too often)

That weak spot is serious. G. William Schwert showed in 1989 that when shocks have a strong negative moving-average component, Phillips-Perron tests can reject a true unit root most of the time. Many applied researchers therefore report ADF as the main test and PP as a robustness check. When the two agree, you can relax. When they disagree, look at the residual autocorrelations before believing either.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text:
There are two ways to deal with a messy memory: describe it (ADF) or measure its total effect and correct for it (PP). Neither is always better. Using both is cheap insurance.

Something to think about

Bill Phillips's MONIAC showed money flowing through an economy, like water. If you could add a tank to the MONIAC that never drains, what kind of time series would its water level be? A kite or a balloon? Leave your answer, and your favourite Phillips, in the comments.

docs.title: Two Courts, Opposite Verdicts: The KPSS Test
docs.text:
Every test we have met so far works like a strict court: the series is presumed to be a random walk, and it is up to the data to prove stationarity beyond reasonable doubt. When the evidence is thin, which it often is, the verdict is "not proven", and lazy researchers write "the series has a unit root".

In 1992 four econometricians asked a cheeky question. What if we built a court with the opposite presumption? Their paper's subtitle says it all: "How sure are we that economic time series have a unit root?"

Unit Root Series · Chapter 5 of 8

1. The kite and the balloon · 2. Dickey-Fuller · 3. Augmented Dickey-Fuller · 4. Phillips-Perron · 5. KPSS · 6. DF-GLS and Ng-Perron · 7. Structural breaks · 8. Panel unit roots

Data: sheets P9_kite_balloon, P11_adf and P14_mystery in blog_datasets.xlsx

docs.title: Four names you will mispronounce
docs.text:
The paper is Kwiatkowski, Phillips, Schmidt and Shin (1992), "Testing the null hypothesis of stationarity against the alternative of a unit root", Journal of Econometrics, volume 54. Everyone calls the test KPSS, partly out of laziness and partly because nobody is sure how to say Kwiatkowski (roughly kfyat-KOF-skee, if you want to impress a Polish friend).

The P is Peter Phillips again, from Chapter 4. By now you may suspect that every unit root test has a Phillips in it somewhere. You would not be far wrong. The S is Peter Schmidt of Michigan State University, and the other S is Yongcheol Shin.

docs.title: The idea: a series made of two parts
docs.text:
KPSS imagine that the series is the sum of a deterministic part, a random walk, and a stationary error:

\[ y_t = \xi\, t + r_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad r_t = r_{t-1} + u_t, \quad \operatorname{Var}(u_t) = \sigma_u^2 \]

The random walk \(r_t\) is the balloon hiding inside the series. Its size is controlled by \(\sigma_u^2\):

  • If \(\sigma_u^2 = 0\), the random walk never moves. \(r_t\) is just a constant, and \(y_t\) is stationary (around a trend if \(\xi \neq 0\)).
  • If \(\sigma_u^2 > 0\), the balloon is inside, and \(y_t\) has a unit root.

So the KPSS null hypothesis is

\[ H_0: \sigma_u^2 = 0 \ (\text{stationary}) \qquad H_1: \sigma_u^2 > 0 \ (\text{unit root}) \]

docs.title: The statistic: watch the running total
docs.text:
Here is the clever part. Regress \(y_t\) on a constant (or a constant and trend) and keep the residuals \(e_t\). Then add them up as you go, a running total:

\[ S_t = e_1 + e_2 + \dots + e_t \]

If the series is stationary, the residuals bounce above and below zero and keep cancelling each other. The running total stays small. If there is a random walk inside, the residuals come in long runs of the same sign (the balloon drifts up for a while, then down), and the running total swings far from zero.

The KPSS statistic measures how big the running total gets:

\[ \eta = \frac{1}{T^2}\, \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} S_t^2}{\hat f_0} \]

where \(\hat f_0\) is the long-run variance of the residuals, estimated with the same Newey-West method as in the Phillips-Perron chapter. Large values of \(\eta\) reject stationarity. It is a Lagrange multiplier (LM) test, which is why EViews labels it "LM-Stat."

The critical values are fixed, and short enough to remember:

Model 10% 5% 1% Constant (level stationary) 0.347 0.463 0.739 Constant + trend (trend stationary) 0.119 0.146 0.216

Careful: KPSS rejects for large values. ADF rejects for large negative values. Students mix these up in exams every single year.

docs.title: Putting the two courts together
docs.text:
Running both tests is called confirmatory analysis. There are four possible outcomes:

KPSS does not reject (looks stationary) KPSS rejects (looks like a unit root) ADF rejects (looks stationary) Stationary. Both agree. Conflict. Check for breaks, outliers or long memory. ADF does not reject (looks like a unit root) The data can't decide. Often too short or too persistent. Unit root. Both agree.

The kite sits in the top-left box. The balloon and GDP sit in the bottom-right box. Those are the comfortable cases.

The uncomfortable case is bottom-left. Here is a series from the sheet P14_mystery: 100 observations, no trend.

  • ADF with a constant: statistic −2.33, p = 0.16. Cannot reject a unit root.
  • KPSS with a constant: η = 0.182. Cannot reject stationarity.

Neither court is willing to convict. This happens a lot with short, persistent series. The data simply don't contain enough information. Is MYSTERY a kite on a very long string, or a balloon? We will crack it in Chapter 6, with sharper tests.

docs.title: Two cautions about KPSS
docs.text:
1. Bandwidth matters. KPSS depends on the long-run variance, which depends on the bandwidth. For a stationary but very persistent series, KPSS tends to reject too often. If KPSS is a close call, try a different bandwidth and see if the verdict survives.
  2. It is not a magic fix. Swapping the null hypothesis does not create information. It only changes who bears the burden of proof. That is exactly why using both tests is more honest than using either alone.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text:
Whenever someone tells you "the series has a unit root because the ADF test could not reject", ask them what KPSS said. A failure to reject is not proof. Two courts with opposite presumptions reaching the same verdict is the closest thing to proof that time series econometrics offers.

Something to think about

You run ADF and KPSS on India's monthly inflation since 2000 and land in the top-right box: ADF says stationary, KPSS says unit root. The RBI adopted a formal inflation target in 2016. Could that explain the conflict? Which test do you think is being fooled, and why? Answer in the comments; Chapter 7 will help.

docs.title: The Short-Sighted Umpire: Power, DF-GLS and the Ng-Perron Tests
docs.text:
Imagine a cricket umpire who is very careful never to give a batsman out wrongly. A noble goal. Unfortunately he achieves it by almost never raising his finger at all. Plumb LBW? "Not out." Edge to the keeper? "Not out, there may have been doubt." He never makes the first kind of mistake. He makes the second kind all day long.

The Dickey-Fuller family of tests is that umpire. In this chapter we measure how short-sighted it is, and meet the tests built to give it glasses.

Unit Root Series · Chapter 6 of 8

1. The kite and the balloon · 2. Dickey-Fuller · 3. Augmented Dickey-Fuller · 4. Phillips-Perron · 5. KPSS · 6. DF-GLS and Ng-Perron · 7. Structural breaks · 8. Panel unit roots

Data: blog_datasets.xlsx, sheet P14_mystery · Simulated, 100 observations

docs.title: Size and power, in plain words
docs.text:
Every test can make two mistakes:

Truth: unit root (balloon) Truth: stationary (kite) Test says "stationary" Type I error. Its chance is the size, set at 5%. Correct. Its chance is the power. Test says "unit root" Correct. Type II error. The short-sighted umpire.

We choose the size ourselves: 5%. The power is whatever the test can manage, and for unit root tests it is often embarrassingly low.

docs.title: Measuring the umpire's eyesight
docs.text:
I simulated 4,000 stationary series of length 100 for each value of \(\rho\) from 0.80 to 1.00, ran two tests on each, and counted how often each test correctly said "stationary":

Read the red line. With \(\rho = 0.92\), the series is genuinely stationary; a shock has a half-life of about 8 periods. Yet the ordinary Dickey-Fuller test spots this only 23% of the time. More than three times out of four it says "unit root" about a series that does not have one. At \(\rho = 0.96\), its power is barely 11%.

Why so bad? Over 100 observations, a kite on a long string and a balloon simply look alike. The string only starts to pull once the kite has drifted far enough, and with \(\rho\) near 1 that takes a long time. The test needs to tell 0.92 from 1.00 using a sample in which the difference has barely had a chance to show.

The blue line is DF-GLS. At \(\rho = 0.92\) it catches the stationary series 47% of the time, about twice as often, while keeping the size near 5% when \(\rho = 1\). Where does the extra power come from?

docs.title: DF-GLS: clean the series first, then test
docs.text:
Graham Elliott, Thomas Rothenberg and James Stock published the idea in Econometrica in 1996. You may know James Stock from the other side of your bookshelf: he is the Stock of Stock and Watson's Introduction to Econometrics.

Their insight is about the constant (and trend). In the ordinary ADF regression, the constant is estimated by OLS alongside everything else. Under a near-unit root, OLS does a poor job of estimating the mean of a series that wanders slowly, and that poor estimate eats into the power of the test.

ERS remove the mean in a smarter way, by GLS detrending. They pick a point "close to" a unit root, a local alternative

\[ \bar\alpha = 1 + \frac{\bar c}{T}, \qquad \bar c = -7 \text{ (constant only)}, \quad \bar c = -13.5 \text{ (constant and trend)} \]

and quasi-difference both the series and the deterministic terms:

\[ \tilde y_1 = y_1, \qquad \tilde y_t = y_t - \bar\alpha\, y_{t-1}\ \ (t \ge 2) \]

They then estimate the mean (and trend) by regressing \(\tilde y_t\) on the quasi-differenced constant (and trend), subtract the fitted deterministic part from \(y_t\), and call the result \(y_t^d\). Finally they run an ADF regression on \(y_t^d\) without any constant:

\[ \Delta y_t^d = \delta\, y_{t-1}^d + \sum_{j=1}^p \gamma_j\, \Delta y_{t-j}^d + \varepsilon_t \]

For \(T = 100\), \(\bar\alpha = 1 - 7/100 = 0.93\). The intuition: estimate the mean as if the series were nearly a random walk, which is exactly the situation in which ordinary OLS struggles.

Where does \(\bar c = -7\) come from?

ERS asked: if we knew the true alternative, what would the most powerful test be? Then they found the single alternative, \(\bar c = -7\) for the constant case, at which a test tuned to it has power of 50% against that alternative. A test tuned to this point turns out to be nearly as good as the best possible test at every alternative. It is like a pair of glasses ground for one distance that happens to work well at most distances.

With only a constant, the DF-GLS statistic follows the Dickey-Fuller distribution for the "no constant" case, so its 5% critical value is about −1.94. With a trend, ERS supply their own table.

ERS also proposed a point-optimal statistic, \(P_T = \left[S(\bar\alpha) - \bar\alpha\, S(1)\right] / \hat f_0\), which compares the sum of squared residuals of the GLS regression under \(\bar\alpha\) and under 1. EViews offers it as "Elliott-Rothenberg-Stock Point-Optimal". Small values reject the unit root.

docs.title: Ng-Perron: four statistics and a better lag rule
docs.text:
Serena Ng and Pierre Perron (2001, Econometrica) took the GLS-detrended series and built four "modified" statistics on it. They also proposed the MAIC lag rule mentioned in Chapter 3. With \(\kappa = T^{-2}\sum_{t=2}^T (y_{t-1}^d)^2\) and \(\hat f_0\) an autoregressive estimate of the long-run variance:

\[ MZ_\alpha = \frac{T^{-1}(y_T^d)^2 - \hat f_0}{2\kappa}, \qquad MSB = \left(\frac{\kappa}{\hat f_0}\right)^{1/2}, \qquad MZ_t = MZ_\alpha \times MSB \]

plus \(MP_T\), a modified version of the ERS point-optimal statistic. You do not need to remember them. Just know three things:

  • They are designed to keep the size honest even when the shocks have the nasty negative moving-average structure that fools Phillips-Perron (Chapter 4).
  • All four reject the unit root for small values. For \(MZ_\alpha\) and \(MZ_t\), small means very negative. For \(MSB\) and \(MP_T\), which are always positive, small means close to zero.
  • Pierre Perron has now appeared in three chapters of this series. He is the Phillips of breakpoints.

docs.title: Is there a catch?
docs.text:
There is always a catch.

  • More power near the unit root sometimes comes with slightly worse size in very small samples, especially with a trend.
  • These tests still assume no structural break. A break can make a kite look like a balloon to every test in this chapter. That's Chapter 7.
  • No test can create information that isn't in the data. With 30 annual observations and \(\rho = 0.95\), even DF-GLS will mostly say "unit root". Sometimes the honest answer is "I can't tell".

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text:
"I could not reject a unit root" often means "my test was short-sighted", not "the series is a random walk". When the stakes are high, use a test with better eyesight. DF-GLS and Ng-Perron are available in the same EViews dialog as ADF, and they cost nothing to run.

Something to think about

Many studies in the 1980s concluded that real exchange rates have unit roots, which would mean purchasing power parity never holds, even in the long run. With what you now know about power, what would you say to the authors of those studies? What kind of data would you want to settle the question? (Hint: Chapter 8.)

docs.title: The Road with a Step: How the Great Crash Rescued the Trend
docs.text:
In 1982 two economists published a paper that shook macroeconomics. Charles Nelson and Charles Plosser took 14 long annual US series, including GNP, industrial production, employment, prices, wages and interest rates, and ran Dickey-Fuller tests on all of them. For all but one, the unemployment rate, they could not reject a unit root.

The conclusion seemed to follow: recessions are not temporary dips below a trend. They are permanent. The economy is a balloon, not a kite. Seven years later, a young Canadian econometrician named Pierre Perron pointed at two dates in history and said: not so fast.

Unit Root Series · Chapter 7 of 8

1. The kite and the balloon · 2. Dickey-Fuller · 3. Augmented Dickey-Fuller · 4. Phillips-Perron · 5. KPSS · 6. DF-GLS and Ng-Perron · 7. Structural breaks · 8. Panel unit roots

Data: blog_datasets.xlsx, sheet P15_break · Simulated annual data, 1960–2023

docs.title: Why Nelson and Plosser mattered
docs.text:
If output is trend-stationary, a recession is a kite in a gust: painful, but the economy returns to its old path. Policy can smooth the ride. If output has a unit root, a recession permanently lowers the path. Part of every shock lasts for ever.

Nelson and Plosser's result was taken as strong support for real business cycle theory, in which fluctuations are driven largely by permanent shocks to technology. The paper, "Trends and random walks in macroeconomic time series" (Journal of Monetary Economics, 1982), became one of the most cited in the field. Charles Plosser later served as President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia from 2006 to 2015. Few econometric papers end with an author helping to set American interest rates.

docs.title: Perron's objection: the Great Crash and the oil shock
docs.text:
Pierre Perron's paper, "The Great Crash, the Oil Price Shock, and the Unit Root Hypothesis" (Econometrica, 1989), made a simple argument.

Suppose a series is a perfectly good kite around a trend, except that once, the trend itself shifted. The string was moved to a new peg. A Dickey-Fuller test fits a single straight trend through the whole sample. After the shift, the series never returns to that line, so the test concludes: "this series does not come back to its trend; it must be a random walk."

Perron treated two events as one-off breaks: the 1929 crash, which lowered the level of most series, and the 1973 oil price shock, which slowed post-war growth. Once he allowed for those breaks, he could reject the unit root for 11 of the 14 Nelson-Plosser series. The economy was a kite after all, just one whose string had been moved twice in a century.

docs.title: Three kinds of break
docs.text:
Perron described three models. Write \(T_B\) for the break date, and define two dummy variables:

\[ DU_t = \begin{cases} 1 & t > T_B \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad DT_t = \begin{cases} t - T_B & t > T_B \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

\(DU_t\) shifts the level of the trend. \(DT_t\) changes its slope. These are the dummy variables of Post 6 again, now moving a trend instead of a seasonal pattern.

Model What changes at the break Extra terms A, the "crash" model The level jumps \(DU_t\) B, the "changing growth" model The slope changes \(DT_t\) C, both Level and slope \(DU_t\) and \(DT_t\)

The test regression for model C looks like an ADF regression with the break terms added:

\[ \Delta y_t = \mu + \beta t + \theta\, DU_t + \gamma\, DT_t + \delta\, y_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^{p} c_j\, \Delta y_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t \]

The unit root test is still the t-statistic on \(\delta\), but with new critical values, because the break terms change the distribution.

docs.title: Zivot and Andrews: don't peek at the date
docs.text:
Perron's critics, Lawrence Christiano among them, raised a fair point. Perron chose 1929 and 1973 after looking at the data. If you get to choose the break after seeing where the series jumps, you will find "evidence" of a break far too easily. It is like drawing the target after shooting the arrow.

Eric Zivot and Donald Andrews answered in 1992, in a paper titled "Further evidence on the great crash, the oil-price shock, and the unit-root hypothesis" (Journal of Business & Economic Statistics). Their fix: let the data pick the break date, and account for the picking in the critical values.

  1. Try every possible break date, leaving out the first and last 15% of the sample.
  2. For each date, run the regression above and record the t-statistic on \(\delta\).
  3. Choose the date where the t-statistic is most negative: the date most favourable to stationarity.
  4. Compare that minimum t-statistic with critical values that allow for the search.

Because we search for the best date, the critical values are more demanding than Perron's. For model C, they are −5.57 at 1%, −5.08 at 5% and −4.82 at 10%. The null hypothesis is a unit root without a break; the alternative is a trend-stationary series with one break at an unknown date.

When Zivot and Andrews re-examined the Nelson-Plosser data this way, fewer series rejected the unit root than in Perron's study. Science is a conversation.

docs.text:
The sheet P15_break has LINCOME, the log of real income per person in an imaginary state, Swarnapur, from 1960 to 2023. I built it as a trend-stationary series (shocks have \(\rho = 0.55\)) with growth of about 1.8% a year. In 1991, an economic reform raises the level of income and lifts the growth rate to about 4.8% a year. There is no unit root anywhere in the true process.

The red dashed line is what an ordinary ADF test with a trend has in mind. The series sits above it until the mid-1970s, falls below it from the late 1970s to the early 2000s, and rises above it again at the end. To the ADF test this looks like wandering. The blue line, with a break in 1991, fits like a glove.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text:
A unit root test sees one straight line. If history put a step in the road, the test will mistake the step for wandering. Before you declare a series a random walk, look at its picture and ask whether something big happened in the middle: a crisis, a reform, a pandemic, a change in how the data are measured.

Something to think about

The Zivot-Andrews test searches for the break that makes the series look most stationary. Suppose the true series is a random walk that happened to fall sharply in 2008. What might the test conclude, and which test in the table above was designed to avoid that mistake? Leave your thoughts in the comments.

docs.title: Twenty States, One Question: Panel Unit Root Tests (and a Field Guide to All of Them)
docs.text:
Chapter 6 ended with a sad fact: with 30 years of annual data, even a good unit root test is half blind. You can't make history longer. But you can look at more places. If you have 30 years of data for 20 states, you have 600 observations of the same economic process playing out in 20 slightly different settings. Can we pool them to see better?

Yes, with care. This final chapter is about panel unit root tests, the tricky questions they answer, and a field guide to every test in this series.

Unit Root Series · Chapter 8 of 8

1. The kite and the balloon · 2. Dickey-Fuller · 3. Augmented Dickey-Fuller · 4. Phillips-Perron · 5. KPSS · 6. DF-GLS and Ng-Perron · 7. Structural breaks · 8. Panel unit roots

Data: blog_datasets.xlsx, sheet P16_panel · Simulated annual panel, 20 states × 1994–2023

docs.title: The data first
docs.text:
The sheet P16_panel has annual inflation for 20 imaginary states, S01 to S20, from 1994 to 2023. I built 17 of them as stationary AR(1) series with \(\rho\) between 0.2 and 0.6. I built the other three, S06, S13 and S18, as random walks.

Can you spot the three random walks without the red colour? It's not easy. S06 drifts up and stays up for a decade; the others are subtle.

docs.title: Testing one state at a time
Pooling: the idea and the catch
docs.text:
Pooling the states gives the test far more information. But it forces us to think hard about a question that single-series tests never raise: what exactly is the alternative hypothesis?

  • "All 20 states are stationary"?
  • "At least some states are stationary"?
  • "All states share the same \(\rho\)"?

Different tests answer different questions. Getting this wrong is the most common mistake with panel unit root tests.

docs.title: Levin, Lin and Chu (2002): one \(\rho\) for everybody
docs.text:
The LLC test runs the ADF regression for every state but forces a common autoregressive coefficient:

\[ \Delta y_{it} = \alpha_i + \delta\, y_{i,t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^{p_i} \gamma_{ij}\, \Delta y_{i,t-j} + \varepsilon_{it} \]

Each state has its own constant \(\alpha_i\) and its own lags, but one \(\delta\). The hypotheses are \(H_0: \delta = 0\) for all states versus \(H_1: \delta < 0\) for all states. Breitung's (2000) test makes the same assumption with a different correction for bias.

The catch: is it believable that the inflation persistence in Kerala and Punjab is exactly the same? Usually not. That's why the next test is more popular.

docs.title: Im, Pesaran and Shin (2003): everyone gets their own \(\rho\)
docs.text:
IPS let each state have its own \(\delta_i\). They simply run a separate ADF test for each state, then average the t-statistics:

\[ \bar t = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} t_i \]

Under the null, every \(t_i\) has a Dickey-Fuller distribution with a known mean and variance (they depend on the sample length and the number of lags). Standardise the average and you get

\[ W_{\bar t} = \frac{\sqrt{N}\,\left(\bar t - \operatorname{E}[t_i]\right)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[t_i]}} \;\sim\; N(0,1) \]

For \(T = 30\) and no lags, \(\operatorname{E}[t_i] \approx -1.52\) and \(\operatorname{Var}[t_i] \approx 0.80\). IPS tabulated these by simulation, much as Dickey and Fuller had done for a single series.

The hypotheses: \(H_0\): every state has a unit root. \(H_1\): some states are stationary. Rejecting the null does not mean all states are stationary.

M. Hashem Pesaran, the P in IPS, has taught at Cambridge and the University of Southern California, and he is one of the most cited econometricians alive. He comes back below.

docs.title: Fisher tests (Maddala and Wu 1999; Choi 2001): combine the p-values
docs.text:
An even simpler idea, borrowed from R. A. Fisher's work in the 1930s on combining independent experiments. Run any unit root test on each state, take its p-value \(p_i\), and combine:

\[ P = -2\sum_{i=1}^{N} \ln p_i \;\sim\; \chi^2_{2N} \] Why does this work? (click to open)

If the null is true, each p-value is uniformly distributed between 0 and 1. For a uniform \(p\), \(-2\ln p\) has a \(\chi^2_2\) distribution. Adding \(N\) independent \(\chi^2_2\) variables gives \(\chi^2_{2N}\). Small p-values make \(-\ln p_i\) big, so many small p-values make \(P\) big.

EViews reports the Fisher test with ADF p-values ("ADF - Fisher Chi-square") and with Phillips-Perron p-values ("PP - Fisher Chi-square"), plus Choi's version \(Z = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum \Phi^{-1}(p_i)\), which is normal under the null. Like IPS, the alternative is "some states are stationary".

docs.title: Hadri (2000): KPSS for panels
docs.text:
Hadri takes the KPSS idea of Chapter 5 to panels. Compute the KPSS statistic \(\eta_i\) for each state, average them, and standardise:

\[ Z = \frac{\sqrt{N}\,\left(\bar\eta - \tfrac16\right)}{\sqrt{1/45}} \;\sim\; N(0,1) \]

(With a constant only, each KPSS statistic has mean 1/6 and variance 1/45 under the null.) The hypotheses are turned around: \(H_0\): every state is stationary. \(H_1\): some states have a unit root.
